name: Omar Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, unions or political parties, and your answers stay confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big press line at Norland Stamping. We stamp steel brackets and panels for washing machines, about nine hundred a shift off my line. I'm senior operator, so I do the die changes, which is swapping the heavy steel shapes that cut the metal, and I sign off the first parts. Six to two, five days, and Saturday mornings when there's overtime.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's honest work. You can see what you made at the end of the day, stacked on pallets. I'm quick on die changes, twenty-two minutes when the manual says forty, and the young ones ask me how. What I don't like is the noise in my ears at night, and that the overtime has been thin since spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Lots of talk, not much change. Sounds about right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it anyway. At the canteen I'd say a press is a press, you still need someone who knows when the steel's off. I'm not online much, maybe the football group, and I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means the same worries as now. The overtime's been thin since the washing machine people moved one model abroad, and without Saturdays I'm short. I live on my own, the rent's most of my pay, and I've got maybe three weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like I am. I'd try to get Saturdays back by asking the supervisor, Mr Hale, to put me on the maintenance overtime list too. And I'd stop buying lunch at the van, which is about thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Nothing's wrong, but nothing's getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overtime has been thin. What does a month without Saturdays look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm counting from the twentieth. Last month I paid the electric late and got a letter. I don't like letters. It's not the end of the world, but still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to if it got worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably. He worked at Norland for twenty-five years before his back went. He'd tell me to keep my head down and wait for the orders to come back.

say: He'd say he **never believed** the AI talk anyway.
A press still needs someone who knows when **the steel's off**.
think: Same worries as now: **overtime** has been thin since a model moved abroad.
Rent takes most of his pay, with about **three weeks** saved.
do: Ask Mr Hale to add him to the **maintenance overtime** list.
Stop buying lunch at the van, about **thirty a week**.
S0.quote: Last month I paid the electric late and got a letter. I don't like letters.
fieldNote: AI barely registers; his real pressure is **lost overtime** and a single income.
He turns to his **father**, a former Norland worker, for advice.
Quiet and **practical**, he wouldn't post opinions online.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hale for a spot on the maintenance overtime list
Pack lunch instead of buying from the van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it hits the office before the floor. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly the office lot who need to worry, which is fair enough, they've had it easy. Then I'd probably feel bad for saying that. At work I'd just tell the young ones to learn the presses properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right for a while, because nobody's putting AI into a die change. But planning tells me what to run, and if a computer does that, it'll squeeze the changeovers harder. And I've seen the robot loaders they put in at the plant in the next valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my numbers good, so I'm the last one they'd let go. I'd try to put the overtime money in the savings account instead of spending it. I wouldn't learn any of the AI stuff, I'd leave that to the people whose job it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the press sounds a bit different and you can't tell why yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the AI tools. Even if Norland asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd do it. But I wouldn't go looking for it. I've never used an AI tool and I don't trust a thing I can't see inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw a robot loader on our line. That's the day I'd start thinking hard. Until then, it's talk.

say: The **office staff** have most to worry about, though he'd regret saying it.
Young operators should **learn the presses** properly.
think: Nobody's putting AI into a **die change**, so he's safe for a while.

do: Keep his **numbers high** so he's the last to go.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a press sounding a bit off.

fieldNote: He sets a clear **trigger**: a robot loader on his own line.
Strong **wait-and-see** instinct; he avoids risk and new tools.
A flash of **resentment** toward office staff, quickly regretted.

steps.text: Keep die-change times under twenty-five minutes
Put overtime pay straight into the savings account
Hold off on AI tools until a robot loader arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not going to happen like that, not round here. Then if it did, I'd say the government had better have something ready, because towns like ours don't have anything else. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 the robots do the presses and I'm out. The die change is the hard part, and I'd bet they'd figure it out. I'd be thirty-one, single, with no savings and a skill nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could for the three years, even move back in with my parents to stop paying rent. I'd ask my uncle about his tiling work, because I can't see robots doing bathrooms in old houses soon. I wouldn't do much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a weight on my chest. I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back home. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing, honestly. I left at twenty-one. But my mum would be happy and I'd save six hundred a month. Pride doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the thinking AI arriving first change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for my hands. The planners and the quality office go first. But when they go, there's nobody left to argue for keeping people on the floor.

say: He'd say it **won't happen** like that round here.
If it did, government must have **something ready** for towns like his.
think: Robots take the presses by **2031** and he's out.

do: **Move back** with his parents to save about six hundred a month.
feel: A **weight** on his chest; he'd **lie awake**.
fieldNote: First reaction is **denial**, then a bleak, specific forecast.
He reaches for **family**: parents for housing, uncle for a trade.
He notices that losing **office staff** removes the people who'd argue for operators.

steps.text: Move back in with his parents to cut six hundred rent
Ask his uncle about learning bathroom tiling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. Still my thirties gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it out properly, so let's see what the government and the company actually do. I'd tell the lads not to panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd wait too long. I know I would. Five years sounds like a lot when you're stamping brackets, and I'd keep thinking the orders would come back. Then 2031 comes, the office empties, and I'd only have three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd carry on at Norland and keep my numbers up. I'd start helping my uncle on Saturday tiling jobs, for cash and to see if I like it. And I'd stop the car finance by selling the car and getting the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a slow way. Like a bill you keep putting in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the car. Would you really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. It's a hundred and forty a month and the bus stops outside Norland. I only kept it for football away games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about it all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him it's not like his day, when Norland was going to be there forever. He'd say that's what they said then too.

He'd tell colleagues **not to panic** yet.
think: He knows he'd **wait too long**, hoping orders return.
Once the office empties in **2031**, he'd have only three years left.
do: Carry on at **Norland** and keep his numbers up.
Help his uncle with **Saturday tiling** for cash.
**Sell the car**, saving a hundred and forty a month.
feel: **Worried** slowly, like a bill left in a **drawer**.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot when you're stamping brackets
fieldNote: Tiling with his uncle becomes a **low-risk test** of a new trade.
Selling the car is a **concrete cut** he's willing to make.

steps.text: Keep running the press line at Norland

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time and people should stop going on about it. Live your life, do your job, and deal with it when it's closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd sit at the back of my mind. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably do nothing for five, then start worrying. But it's also long enough to learn tiling properly or get a ticket for something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Norland, that's the main thing. I'd do the Saturday tiling with my uncle when he needs a hand. Around year three, if the robot loaders started showing up in the valley, I'd do a proper tiling course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd put it out of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it out of your mind. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My dad put things out of his mind until his back went. Then it was too late to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably hold off on getting a mortgage. Thirty years of mortgage payments when the job might go at thirty-seven? No.

People should live their lives and **deal with it** when it's closer.

Ten years is enough to **learn tiling** properly.

Take a **tiling course** around year three if robot loaders appear.

fieldNote: Public line is **dismissive**, private line admits drift.
His father's **missed chance** is a quiet warning he carries.
The long timeline changes a **life decision**: delaying a mortgage.

steps.text: Keep working the press line at Norland

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years till the robots, no savings, and I'm not a quick learner with new things. What would help is someone telling me straight which trades will still be there, and paying me while I learn one. I don't need a speech, I need a list and a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the noise. I've got ringing ears at twenty-seven. If a robot does the press, at least the next lad keeps his hearing.

headlineQuote: I don't need a speech, I need a list and a wage.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** senior press operator at Norland Stamping, making washing machine brackets.
He lives **alone**, with rent taking most of his pay and about three weeks saved.
Pragmatic and **cautious**, he never uses AI and admits he'd wait too long.
He leans on **family**: his father's advice, his parents' home and his uncle's tiling work.
He's **alarmed** by the two-year warning; with longer warnings he drifts and delays.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots in three years and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **list** of lasting trades and a **wage** while learning one.
